item.title: Managing Under Political Turbulence
item.content:encoded:
Jonathan Doh, Villanova University

Srividya Jandhyala, ESSEC Business School

Yadong Luo, University of Miami

Grazia D. Santangelo, Copenhagen Business School

Political turbulence is on the rise, as evidenced most dramatically in violent conflicts (e.g., wars, terrorism attacks), volatile political transitions (e.g., dramatic regime change, cuts to government employees, new geopolitical alliances, coups), and geopolitical tensions (e.g., trade wars, democratic backsliding, sanctions). This escalated political turbulence exacerbates geopolitical risks for organizations and their stakeholders.

Whether anticipatory (e.g., fear of cyberattacks) or actual (e.g., ongoing trade wars, competition over territories), rising geopolitical risks affect organizations in many ways. The rise of techno-nationalism, driven by national security and ideological concerns, challenges the resilience of global technology supply chains. With the rapid development of AI comes misinformation and disinformation that further aggravate political tensions and ideologies. Tariffs, sanctions, and protectionist trade restrictions bring escalating compliance risks. Rising populist sentiment drives immigration restrictions and is creating a shortage of high-skill talent for MNEs.

item.title: Turning Implications Into Evidence: Actionable Solutions to Real-World Problems of Practice and Policy Based on Prior Academy of Management Publications
item.content:encoded:
Julian Birkinshaw, Western University

Thomas P. Lyon, University of Michigan

Denise M. Rousseau, Carnegie Mellon University

Majken Schultz, Copenhagen Business School

Mo Wang, University of Florida

Amid rising concern about the relevance of their contents, many scholarly journals mandate inclusion of a managerial implications section. This section may be relegated to a few paragraphs at the end of an article and comprised of speculative statements loosely connected to the paper's empirical or theoretical content. And there these unvalidated implications tend to remain, largely unaddressed in future research studies and having little relevance to practice or policy.

This special issue calls for original research that develops actionable solutions from previously published managerial implications. By developing actionable insights from underdeveloped or dormant implications, this special issue furthers the core function of any science: the development of a corpus of valid and reliable knowledge. An applied science has the added demand that knowledge be usable outside of academia.

Potential topics

  • Developing actionable solutions from previously published managerial implications
  • Novel empirical or conceptual analysis of practice and policy implications
  • Real-world problems of practice and policy overlooked in managerial implications sections
  • Robust analysis providing specific guidance for practitioners and policy makers
  • Building on theory developed in Academy of Management journals to enrich and reveal nuances of their usefulness

item.title: Open Call for Papers
item.content:encoded:
Academy of Management Perspectives (AMP) publishes papers that matter to managers. The journal seeks to realize the field's long-standing call for managerially relevant work. AMP papers must be managerially driven from the start, not theory-driven papers with managerial implications added as an afterthought. Papers rejected from theory-focused journals are not suitable for AMP unless they are fundamentally reoriented toward managerial relevance.

AMP papers must meet three core criteria: they must be RELEVANT, RIGOROUS, and READABLE. Relevant papers inform an issue of evident importance to managerial practice and/or policy. Rigorous papers engage in rigorous and original conceptual or empirical analysis. Readable papers concisely and clearly convey key ideas to a non-specialized audience. All three criteria must be satisfied.

Potential topics

  • Papers that inform managerial practice and policy
  • Work addressing issues of evident importance to managerial practice and/or policy
  • Rigorous and original conceptual or empirical analysis
  • Papers accessible to non-specialized audiences and practitioners
  • Work grounded in evidence or robust conceptual frameworks
  • Papers offering actionable insights for managers and policymakers
